books.title: Start With Why
books.author: Simon Sinek
books.description: Why some leaders inspire action while others don't, built around the idea of the Golden Circle.
ideas: Start with why
Most organizations explain what they do and how they do it. Inspiring leaders start with why: the purpose or belief behind the work. People don't just buy what you do; they buy into why you do it.
start-with-why
The Golden Circle
Picture three rings: why at the centre, how around it and what on the outside. Inspiring communication moves from the inside out.
Manipulation versus inspiration
Discounts, fear and peer pressure can drive a sale, but they don't build loyalty. Shared belief does.
Trust comes from consistency
When what you say and what you do line up with your why, people trust you. Clarity, discipline and consistency keep the circle balanced.

books.title: Extreme Ownership
books.author: Jocko Willink & Leif Babin
books.description: Two former Navy SEAL officers apply battlefield leadership lessons to business and life.
ideas: Own everything in your world

When something goes wrong, a good leader doesn't blame the team, the plan or bad luck. They take responsibility, find what they could have done better and fix it. That ownership spreads through the whole team.
extreme-ownership
No bad teams, only bad leaders
The same team can fail or succeed depending on who leads it. Standards are what the leader tolerates.
Prioritize and execute
When overwhelmed, step back, pick the single highest-priority problem, solve it, then move to the next. Trying to fix everything at once fixes nothing.
Simple plans win
Complex plans fall apart under pressure. If everyone can't understand the plan, it's too complicated.
Decentralized command
Leaders explain the intent, then let people closest to the action make decisions. Teams move faster when they don't wait for approval.

books.title: Leaders Eat Last
books.author: Simon Sinek
books.description: Why the best teams feel safe, and how leaders create that circle of safety.
ideas: The circle of safety
When people feel protected by their leader from threats inside the organization, they focus their energy on outside challenges instead of on watching their backs.
Leadership is a choice
Rank doesn't make someone a leader. Choosing to look after the people around you does.
Leaders take the hit
In the military, officers traditionally eat after their troops. Good leaders give up some of their own comfort for the people they're responsible for.
People are not numbers
When leaders treat people as costs on a spreadsheet, trust collapses. Seeing them as humans builds loyalty that money can't buy.

books.title: Dare to Lead
books.author: Brené Brown
books.description: A researcher on vulnerability explains the courage-building skills behind brave leadership.
ideas: Clear is kind
Being vague to avoid an awkward conversation is unkind. Clear expectations and honest feedback, delivered with respect, help people succeed.
Vulnerability is courage
Saying "I don't know" or "I was wrong" takes courage. Leaders who can be vulnerable make it safe for others to take risks.
Armoured versus daring leadership
Perfectionism, cynicism and needing to be right are armour. They protect the leader but stop the team from learning.
Name your values
Choose two core values and define what they look like in action. Values only count when they guide hard decisions.

books.title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
books.author: Patrick Lencioni
books.description: A leadership fable about the five problems that keep teams from working together.
ideas: Absence of trust
When team members can't admit mistakes or weaknesses, everyone wastes energy protecting themselves. Trust is the foundation of every other team skill.
Fear of conflict
Teams without trust avoid open debate. Artificial harmony leads to poor decisions because real concerns are never voiced.
Lack of commitment
If people haven't had a chance to weigh in, they won't truly buy in, even if they nod in the meeting.
Avoidance of accountability
When commitment is fuzzy, peers hesitate to call each other out. Standards slip quietly.
Inattention to results
When individuals care more about their status or department than team goals, collective results suffer.

books.title: The Art of War
books.author: Sun Tzu
books.description: An ancient Chinese treatise on strategy that is still read by leaders far beyond the military.
ideas: Know yourself and your opponent
If you know both yourself and the other side, you need not fear the outcome of a hundred battles. Most failures come from ignoring one of the two.
Win without fighting
The highest skill is to achieve your goal without open conflict, by outmanoeuvring, persuading or making the fight unnecessary.
Attack weakness, avoid strength
Like water flowing downhill, strategy should flow around strong points and toward weak ones.
Speed and preparation
Victory usually goes to whoever prepared more thoroughly beforehand. Battles are won before they begin.
